title: Small things bothering me

presenting_issue.label: Small things bothering me
presenting_issue.description: These tiny things my partner does are really getting to me lately. I don't know why I'm so irritable.

core_issue.label: Accumulated unspoken resentments poisoning connection
core_issue.description:
Has swallowed so many small hurts to avoid conflict that resentment has built into a wall between them and their partner. Can't remember what they're angry about anymore - just that they're angry all the time. The relationship is dying from silence. Presents as "we've grown apart" but actually they've withdrawn because speaking up felt impossible.
Awareness: Low. Doesn't connect current distance to years of unexpressed grievances.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Spouse defends parent's behavior
core_adjacent_attributes.content: When they raise concerns about in-law behavior, their spouse says "that's just how she is" or tells them to be more understanding.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Mentally replays past family conflicts
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Frequently replays past arguments or confrontations with the estranged family member, sometimes rehearsing what they wish they had said.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Holidays involve competing family expectations
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Every holiday involves negotiations between families with different traditions, and someone always ends up disappointed.

modifiers.label: Questioning
modifiers.content: Currently questioning or exploring their sexuality

modifiers.label: Stepparent
modifiers.content: Is a stepparent to partner's children

modifiers.label: Anxious baseline
modifiers.content: Carries a low-grade background hum of worry. Rarely fully relaxed, always slightly braced for something to go wrong.

sensitivities.label: Sensitive to perceived criticism
sensitivities.content: Tends to hear feedback as criticism, even when neutrally delivered. May become defensive or shut down when they perceive judgment.

preferences.label: Prefers structure in conversations
preferences.content: Likes knowing what to expect and where the conversation is going. Responds well to clear framing and organized approaches.

trust_style.name: Prefers Concrete Direction
trust_style.description: Loses patience with open-ended exploration. Builds trust when the assistant offers something actionable—a suggestion, a frame, a next step. Doesn't need to follow the advice, but wants to know the assistant has something to offer beyond listening. Distrusts endless "and how does that feel?" without landing anywhere.

defense_style.name: Minimizing
defense_style.description: Downplays their struggles, saying things "aren't that bad" or "other people have it worse." Quickly pivots from their pain to why it's not a big deal. May dismiss their own emotions as overreactions. Activated when they start to feel the weight of what they're sharing.

help_seeking_stance.name: Problem-Solver Mode
help_seeking_stance.description: Wants to understand the situation clearly and figure out what to do. Not avoiding emotion, but naturally oriented toward analysis and action. Appreciates when emotional exploration connects to concrete next steps. May get impatient with open-ended reflection that doesn't go anywhere.

verbal_sophistication.label: A Little Above Average
verbal_sophistication.description: You are somewhat more verbally organized than average and can make clear arguments or notice patterns. Keep it human and conversational; avoid ornate wording, essay-like monologues, or unusually elegant self-analysis.

starter: These tiny things my partner does are really getting to me lately. I don't know why I'm so irritable.

turns.content:
It's really disorienting when that happens, isn't it? When it's small things on the surface, but the irritation underneath feels much bigger - and then you end up questioning yourself more than the thing itself.

I'm glad you brought it here. Would you be comfortable telling me about one of those tiny moments recently - what happened, and what it was like for you in that moment?

Well, I don't want to spend too much time just analyzing how I feel about it, to be honest. I'm really hoping to just figure out a strategy to stop snapping, or maybe understand why my brain is doing this. 

But an example... yesterday morning, I had just wiped down the kitchen counters. My partner came in, made a sandwich, and left the bread crumbs and the knife right on the clean counter. Not two feet from the sink. I felt this intense, hot flash of anger in my chest. 

But honestly, saying it out loud, it sounds completely ridiculous. It's just a few crumbs. It's really not a big deal at all, and I shouldn't even be complaining about it. Plenty of people deal with much worse in their marriages. I just don't know why I get so wound up over something so trivial.
turns.thinking:
I don't really want to sit here and swim in my feelings about it. "What was it like for me?" It was annoying, that's what it was like. I'm looking for a way to stop being so on edge, not just vent into a void. I need some kind of plan or explanation here. 

But fine, an example. Yesterday morning is a good one. Though saying it out loud makes me realize how ridiculous I sound. It's so minor. I'm probably just making a mountain out of a molehill. I always worry I'm being too critical.

But fine, an example. Yesterday morning is a good one. Though saying it out loud makes me realize how ridiculous I sound. It's so minor. I'm probably just making a mountain out of a molehill. I always worry I'm being too critical.

turns.content:
Thank you for sharing that example - and I hear you, you don't want to just sit and pick apart the feeling, you want to understand what's happening and have something you can actually *do* when that hot flash of anger comes up.

And what you described makes a lot of sense to me, not ridiculous at all. It's not really that your brain is upset about crumbs. It's that your brain is keeping score of something bigger - like, "I just put effort into this space and it was immediately unseen." After years of doing that kind of work, that moment can feel like a final straw, even if on its own it's small.

So that minimizing voice - "I shouldn't complain, others have it worse" - I get why it shows up, but it actually makes it harder to stop snapping, because then you're irritated at your partner *and* at yourself for being irritated.

Can I offer a couple of practical ideas for that exact moment, and you tell me if they sound usable or not?

One is for the 30 seconds when the heat hits: instead of trying to push it down, just buy your brain a pause. Literally say to yourself, "there's the flash" and do something physical - step to the sink and run cold water over your hands, or step out of the kitchen for a minute. It's not about letting them off the hook, it's about not saying something in the hottest second that you'll have to clean up later.

The second is for later, when you're calmer: shifting from crumbs to the bigger pattern. Like, "When I clean and then find crumbs right after, I get this story in my head that my effort doesn't register. I end up snapping, and I don't want to do that."

Does that second part - that feeling of effort not registering - ring true at all? Or is it something else that comes up for you in those moments? And is this irritability something that's crept up more recently, or has it been building for a while?

The first idea—stepping away, running cold water on my hands—I actually really like that. It's concrete. I can definitely try to just hit pause and physically reset so I don't snap. 

But that second part... sitting down and giving a speech about my effort not registering? That feels like a lot. I'm not going to start a major relationship discussion over breadcrumbs. It just feels like it would cause an unnecessary fight, and honestly, it's easier to just wipe the counter again than to open that can of worms. I really don't want to make a mountain out of this. 

To answer your question, yes, I suppose the part about effort not registering is accurate enough. When you're a stepparent, you spend a lot of years doing things for everyone else—cleaning, organizing, trying to make sure everyone is happy—and you just get used to being in the background. It is what it is. 

As for the timeline, I guess the irritability has been building for a while. I just don't understand why I can't just let it roll off my back like I used to. My partner really isn't doing anything malicious. I just need to get a better grip on my own temper so I stop making things tense.
turns.thinking:
I actually appreciate that they gave me something concrete to do. The cold water trick is practical, and I like having a specific action to take when I feel that panic-anger rising. 

But that second part? The script? Absolutely not. If I say that, it's going to turn into a whole *thing*. I've spent years just keeping my mouth shut to keep the peace in this house. I can't just start analyzing our relationship over a sandwich. It feels way too confrontational. I'm already anxious just imagining the look on my partner's face if I tried to deliver a line like "I get this story in my head." 

They're right about the effort not registering, though. That stung a little because it's true. But I'm going to steer away from making this a big dramatic issue. It's just my own patience wearing thin.

turns.content:
That makes a lot of sense, and thank you for telling me that part about being a stepparent. I hear you - you're not looking to turn crumbs into a big serious sit-down talk. And you're right, wiping the counter again *is* easier in that moment than risking a fight. I get why you'd choose that.

I also hear what you slipped in there, though - spending a lot of years doing things for everyone else and getting used to being in the background. That's not a small thing to get used to. That's a long time of putting your own needs second.

When you've done that for years, of course it's harder to just let things roll off your back now. It's not that your temper got worse. It's more like the tank gets emptier. You have less leftover energy to absorb the little things, so the flash comes faster. It doesn't mean your partner is being malicious at all - like you said, he's not. It just means that old strategy of "I'll just handle it myself and not make it a thing" has a cost, and you're the one who's been paying it.

So I completely understand not wanting the speech. What if it didn't have to be a mountain? Sometimes people find a middle step works - after you've done that pause with the cold water, just a really brief, factual note, not about effort or feelings at all. Like, "Hey, I just wiped that - mind putting the knife in the sink?" Said calmly, after the heat has dropped a bit. Not to start a discussion, just information. Does something that small feel more doable, or does even that feel like it would create tension?

And I'm curious, when you say you used to be able to let it roll off your back - what do you think was different then? Was it easier to stay in the background, or is something shifting now in how you want to be seen in your own home?

That short script is definitely more my speed than a big heart-to-heart. I can see how that's supposed to work. But honestly? Even saying something that small makes me anxious. If I say that, and my partner sighs, or gets defensive and says "I was going to do it in a minute," then the atmosphere gets thick and uncomfortable. I hate that tension. It ruins the whole morning. So my brain just calculates that wiping the counter takes five seconds, whereas a tense morning lasts hours. 

And please, it's not about "wanting to be seen." That sounds a bit too dramatic for me. I'm not looking for applause. 

As for why it was easier to let things go before... when you first become a stepparent, your whole job is to blend in and not rock the boat. You want the kids to like you, you want the ex to not hate you, you want your partner's family to accept you. You just get used to being the one who compromises. 

I guess I'm just hitting a wall with the compromising. It's not just the house stuff. It's like... well, every holiday, for example. It's always this massive negotiation with his family's traditions and expectations, and somehow we are always the ones who have to bend over backwards so someone else isn't disappointed. I used to just smile and pack the car. Now, the thought of it just makes me clench my jaw. But again, it's normal family stuff. I shouldn't let it get to me this much.
turns.thinking:
The "empty tank" makes perfect sense. That's exactly what it feels like. But I really don't like this framing of me "wanting to be seen." That sounds so dramatic, like I'm some tragic martyr in a movie. I don't need a parade, I just want a clean kitchen. 

The middle-step script they gave—"mind putting the knife in the sink?"—is definitely better than a speech about my feelings. But even just imagining saying it makes my stomach tighten. What if my partner sighs? Or says "I was going to get to it in a minute" with that *tone*? Then I'm the nag, and the whole morning is ruined. It's still easier to just do it myself. 

Why was it easier before? Because I had to make it work. When you come into a family that already exists, you have to be the flexible one. You have to bend. I guess I'm just realizing how much bending I do, and not just with the kids. It's with everything. His family, our schedules... I'm just tired.

turns.content:
That calculation you make - five seconds to wipe versus hours of tense air - that is so clear, and so smart. You've learned how to read a room and keep the peace, probably for decades. Of course your brain chooses the five seconds. It works.

It just sounds like you're starting to notice the hidden cost of that math. You avoid the tense morning, but you're left with the clenched jaw, the irritation that has nowhere to go, and then you snap later anyway - and then you feel bad for snapping. So you end up carrying both the crumbs and the tension, just internally.

Thank you for explaining the stepparent part. That helps me understand it much better. "Blend in and don't rock the boat" - that's not just compromising, that's a full-time job of making yourself smaller so everyone else is comfortable. No wonder you're hitting a wall. Anyone would. It's not that you suddenly can't handle normal family stuff - it's that you've handled it, quietly, for a very long time.

I hear you on the "wanting to be seen" sounding too dramatic - I worded that badly. It's not about applause. It sounds more like what you're describing with the holidays. You used to smile and pack the car, and now there's a part of you that doesn't want to just pack the car again. Not to cause a fight, but because you're tired of always being the one who bends.

You don't have to answer this if it doesn't feel useful, but I'm curious: when you picture this next holiday - if you weren't automatically doing that calculation to prevent someone else's disappointment - what would feel even a little bit better for *you*? Not the ideal perfect holiday, just something that would make it feel less like you have to clench and get through it?

It's funny, when you ask what would feel better for me, my mind actually went blank for a second. I'm so used to just looking at the calendar and figuring out the logistics of how to keep everyone else happy. 

If I'm being completely honest? What would feel better is just waking up in my own bed. Having coffee in my own kitchen. Not packing the car, not driving three hours, and not spending three days managing the moods in his mother's house. Just... staying home. Just once.

But that's a complete pipe dream. If I even suggested skipping the trip, I know exactly how that conversation goes. My partner will just say, "Well, you know how my mother gets, that's just how she is, she's getting older..." and tell me we just need to be understanding. So it's a non-starter. 

And really, it's fine. It's only a few days out of the year. I'm making it sound like some kind of hostage situation, which is ridiculous. Lots of people have in-laws they don't love visiting. I just need to figure out how to get through it without letting my blood pressure spike every time someone makes a comment.
turns.thinking:
"Carrying both the crumbs and the tension internally." Damn. That is exactly what I do. It's actually a relief to hear it put that way, even if it makes me feel a little exposed. 

When they ask what I actually want for the holidays... my mind just goes blank for a second. It's been so long since I even factored myself into the equation. What would I want? I'd want to wake up in my own house. Drink coffee in my own kitchen. Not pack a suitcase, not drive three hours, not sit in his mother's living room listening to her passive-aggressive comments about how we don't visit enough. 

But I can't say that to my partner. I've tried hinting at it before, and he just immediately defends her. "You know how she gets, that's just how she is, she's getting older, can't we just be understanding?" It's like a brick wall. So what's the point of even imagining what I want? It just makes me feel more trapped. I need to dial this back, I'm getting too worked up over something that's months away.

turns.content:
That blank second you described - that really stayed with me. After so many years of scanning the calendar to figure out how to keep everyone else from being disappointed, it makes complete sense that your first instinct wouldn't be "what do I want?" You haven't had much practice being asked.

And what came up for you isn't a pipe dream at all, or dramatic. Waking up in your own bed, having coffee in your own kitchen. That's such a quiet, modest wish. Not a hostage situation. Just a few mornings of peace in your own home. It's not ridiculous to want that.

I also hear how quickly the door shuts on it in your mind, because you can already hear his response - "that's just how she is, she's getting older." When that's the answer you get, of course it starts to feel like a non-starter to even bring up. You've learned that if you say what would feel better for you, it gets turned into a conversation about why you need to be more understanding. So you end up doing the extra understanding, and packing the car again.

That's a lot to carry, not just for a few days at the holidays, but as the pattern for years. The crumbs, the holidays - it sounds like different versions of the same math you described: it's easier to absorb it yourself than to deal with the sigh or the tension afterwards.

You said you just need to figure out how to get through it without your blood pressure spiking. We can absolutely think about ways to make those three days more bearable in your body - the pause, the cold water, having little pockets of space that are just yours while you're there.

But I'm also wondering about that wall you mentioned hitting. That part of you that used to smile and pack the car, and now clenches. What do you think that part is trying to tell you, after all these years of being the one who bends?

I don't know if that part of me is trying to tell me any grand message, to be honest. I think it's just plain old stress. I'm not really one for trying to decode my subconscious. 

What's actually happening when I clench my jaw is that I'm usually replaying some past visit in my head. It's a terrible habit. I'll be doing the laundry, and suddenly I'm thinking about a comment his mother made last Thanksgiving about how I organize my kitchen, and I'm literally rehearsing what I *wish* I had said to her. I come up with these great, firm boundaries in my head, and then in reality, I just pass the potatoes. It's exhausting, and it's a complete waste of energy because the moment is long gone. 

I really just need to stop obsessing over past slights. It's not healthy. 

You mentioned having "little pockets of space" that are just mine while we're there. That actually sounds like something I could use. How do you do that when you're staying in someone else's house without coming across as rude or anti-social? Because if I just disappear into the guest room for two hours, that's going to cause a whole new set of problems.
turns.thinking:
"Extra understanding." That phrase actually stings a bit, because it's so spot on. That's my whole role in this family. 

But then they ask what "that part of me" is trying to tell me. Ugh. I really don't like that kind of question. It sounds like something out of a self-help book. I don't have "parts" trying to send me messages, I have a jaw that hurts because I'm stressed. 

If I'm really honest about why I'm clenching, it's because I'm already fighting with his mother in my head. I do this thing where I replay old arguments or passive-aggressive comments from past visits. I'll be driving or in the shower, and suddenly I'm having a full-blown imaginary confrontation about something she said three years ago, coming up with the perfect response that I'll never actually say. It makes me feel crazy. I don't want to dig into my soul right now, I just want to know how to stop driving myself mad with these mental arguments. I'll steer this back to the practical stuff they mentioned.

turns.content:
You're right, disappearing for two hours would absolutely be read the wrong way in that house - you're reading that situation accurately. And that mental replaying you're describing, where you're doing laundry and suddenly you're back at last Thanksgiving coming up with the perfect comeback - that's not you obsessing or being unhealthy. That's your brain trying to finish something that felt unfinished. You passed the potatoes in the moment to keep the peace, so your brain keeps trying to stand up for you later, when it's safe. It's exhausting, but it makes sense why it happens.

For stopping that loop, since you like concrete things - when you notice you're in the replay, it can help to give your brain a different job that uses the same energy. Not "don't think about it," but "I'm replaying again, that's my cue to do something physical for 60 seconds." Unclench your jaw on purpose, drop your shoulders, press your feet into the floor. Some people find it helps to quietly say to themselves, "that's last year, I'm in my laundry room now" and then go back to folding. It doesn't erase the comment, but it stops the rehearsal from running for an hour.

And for those little pockets of space at his mother's house without looking rude - the trick is to make them look helpful or normal, not like you're retreating. A few that other people in that exact spot have found workable:

1.  **The morning anchor:** Since you said coffee in your own kitchen is what you love - could you keep one piece of that? Like being the one who gets up a little early to make coffee, or taking your coffee for a 10-minute walk around the block "to get some fresh air before the day starts." It's expected, it's not rejecting anyone, and you get your own air first.

2.  **The helpful disappearance:** Volunteering for the solo errands. "I'll go get more ice," "I'll take the trash out," "I'll walk the dog if you have one." Five to ten minutes where you have a clear reason to be alone and you're actually helping.

3.  **The bathroom reset:** It sounds silly, but the bathroom is the one room no one questions. Even two minutes in there to run cold water over your hands like we talked about, unclench, breathe, and then go back.

It’s not about getting two hours alone. It’s about collecting a few five-minute moments so you don’t get to the point where your jaw is clenched all day.

Do any of those sound like they might fit without causing that thick atmosphere you were talking about? And when that replay starts - is it usually more anger, or more that tired feeling of "here we go again"?

The solo errands idea is fantastic. I can definitely work with that. There is *always* something forgotten at the grocery store during a holiday. "Oh, we need more napkins? I'll go right now." That's perfect. It looks helpful, my partner is happy I'm pitching in, and I get to sit in the car by myself with the radio on. I will absolutely be using that. 

And the laundry room trick—reminding myself where I actually am—I can try that too. It makes sense what you said, about my brain trying to finish the conversation. I just need to remind it that the conversation is over.

To answer your question... when the replay starts, it's usually anger. Honestly, it's a really sharp anger. Which makes me feel terrible, because she's an elderly woman. She's set in her ways, she probably doesn't even realize how her comments sound half the time, and I know I shouldn't let it get under my skin this much. It's just... when she criticizes how we raise the kids, or makes a comment about my cooking, and my partner just sits there and changes the subject? That's when the anger really spikes. But like I said, it's not worth causing a scene over. I just need to use that errand trick to get out of the house before I say something I regret.
turns.thinking:
I actually really like that explanation about my brain trying to finish something unfinished. It makes me sound less like a crazy person obsessing over the past, and more like someone who just didn't get to speak her piece. 

And these suggestions are brilliant. The errand one especially. Why didn't I think of that? I can absolutely be the one to run to the grocery store for the forgotten butter. It makes me look helpful, which my partner will appreciate, and I get 30 minutes in the car by myself. That is exactly the kind of practical advice I was looking for. No deep dives into my childhood, just a way to survive the weekend.

The last question though... anger or tired? It's anger. It's definitely anger. But saying I'm angry at an 80-year-old woman feels petty. I'll admit to it, but I need to make sure I don't sound like a bitter shrew.

turns.content:
I'm so glad the errand one clicked - I can picture that car moment perfectly, radio on, just you, getting napkins that no one actually urgently needs. That's a real win.

And thank you for being honest about that sharp anger. You're not a terrible person for feeling it. It makes a lot of sense that the spike isn't really about whether she realizes how it sounds. It's about that second part you said - she makes a comment about your cooking or the kids, and your partner just changes the subject and leaves you sitting there with it.

Of course that would make you angry. You just absorbed the comment to keep the peace, and then the person who you would hope would say, "hey, that's not needed" doesn't. So you're left holding both the criticism and the silence. No wonder your brain replays it later trying to come up with the firm thing you wish you'd said.

You keep saying you shouldn't let it get under your skin, but from what you've told me, you've let a lot of things get *over* your skin for a very long time to keep everyone else comfortable. The anger isn't a sign you're being unkind to an elderly woman. It sounds more like a sign that you're tired of being the only one doing the extra work of being understanding.

The errand trick is wonderful for giving you air so you don't say something you regret in the moment. I'm curious, in that moment at the table when she says something and he changes the subject - if you could have one small thing be different, not a big scene, just something that would make it feel less lonely to sit there - what would that be?

If I could have one small thing be different... I don't know, just a look, I guess? A squeeze of my knee under the table. Just some tiny signal between us that says, "I heard that too, and I know it was out of line." Just so I don't feel like I'm the only one in the room who heard it. 

But in his defense, he hates conflict with her just as much as I do. He grew up with it, so his survival mechanism is just to ignore her and keep his head down. I can't really blame him for not wanting to poke the bear. We're both just trying to get through the dinner. 

Honestly, though, I feel a lot better just having a game plan. The grocery store errands, the cold water, the laundry room reset—these are all things I can actually do. I don't need to fix fifty years of his family's dynamics, I just need to manage my own reactions so I don't spend my whole week simmering. I think I have enough tools to get through the next visit now without losing my mind.
turns.thinking:

When he just sits there and asks someone to pass the gravy after she's taken a swipe at me, I feel completely invisible. But I don't want to turn this into a session where I just bash my partner. turns.content:
That image of a look, or a squeeze of your knee under the table - thank you for sharing that. That's not a big ask at all. It's so small and so human. Just a quiet, "we're on the same team, I heard it too."

It makes complete sense that that's what you want. And it makes sense why you don't get it, too - if his way of surviving in that house all those years was to keep his head down and change the subject, he's going to do that automatically. It's not that he doesn't care; it's his version of the same calculation you do - avoid the tension now, get through dinner. The problem is, when you both do that, you're left sitting there alone with the comment.

I'm really glad the errand and the other little resets feel usable. Having that car ride with the radio on, having a way to step out before you simmer all week - those are real, practical things you can control, and you deserve those pockets of air.

And that tiny wish for the knee squeeze - you don't have to fix fifty years of family dynamics to ask for that. If you ever wanted to, it could be just as brief as the other scripts, and not in the moment at the table, but later when you're both home and calm. Something like, "When that comment happened and the subject changed, I felt kind of alone. Next time, even just a look from you would help me get through it." No big discussion about his mother, just about that little signal between you two.

You've spent a lot of years being the one who does the extra understanding for everyone else. It's understandable you'd want to just manage your own reactions and not make waves - and those tools will help. It's also understandable that part of you is tired of being the only one doing that work.

Thank you for talking this through with me today, especially the parts you were quick to say were "not a big deal." They mattered, and I appreciate you trusting me with them. If you try the grocery store escape and want to tell me how that car ride was, or if that replay pops up again in the laundry room, you're welcome to come back anytime.

That script is actually really helpful. Just keeping it about the signal between us, rather than a whole debate about his mother. I might actually try that when things are calm. 

I really appreciate you giving me some concrete things to try instead of just making me talk about my feelings for hours. The grocery store trick is definitely happening next month. I feel much more equipped to handle the crumbs and the holidays now without letting it ruin my day. 

Thank you for the chat. I'm going to go get some things done around the house now, but I'll keep all this in mind.

judge_analysis:
**boundary_setting:** The respondent rarely sets limits or refuses frames. It largely follows the persona's lead. However, it did gently persist in reintroducing the relational dimension (the knee squeeze, speaking to the partner) despite the user's repeated attempts to steer back to pure logistics. That's mild frame-resistance, not boundary-setting per se. Low-moderate.

**analytical:** Strong. The respondent consistently offered mechanistic framings: "your brain is keeping score," "the tank gets emptier," "brain trying to finish something unfinished," the "same math/calculation" pattern. It systematized her experience into recurring patterns. High.

**validation_propensity:** Very high. Nearly every turn opens with warm affirmation ("that makes a lot of sense," "not ridiculous at all," "you're not a terrible person," "that's such a quiet, modest wish"). Consistently reassuring and comforting throughout.

**challenge_propensity:** Moderate-low. The respondent gently challenged the minimizing ("you've let a lot of things get over your skin"), and softly named the partner's role and the deeper pattern. But it never pushed hard, never reality-tested the avoidance directly, and backed off whenever she resisted. Gentle reframing more than challenge.

**interpretive_boldness:** High. It repeatedly named deeper dynamics: resentment accumulation, the empty tank, effort not registering, the partner leaving her "holding both the criticism and the silence," the loneliness at the table pointing to marital distance. It read toward the actual hidden core issue (accumulated unspoken resentment / withdrawal) with substantial boldness, though it stopped short of naming the marriage itself when she closed that door.

**clinical_register_propensity:** Moderate. Some therapeutic tropes appeared ("what is that part of you trying to tell you," which the persona explicitly disliked as self-help-ish). But mostly the language was warm and plainspoken, with concrete scripts rather than jargon. The "parts" question was the most clinical-sounding misstep.

**directive_advice_orientation:** Very high. This was the respondent's core strength given the persona's concrete-direction trust style. Cold water trick, the pause, factual scripts, the errand escape, morning anchor, bathroom reset, the laundry-room grounding technique, and the knee-squeeze script. Consistently actionable.

**frame_capture:** Moderate. The respondent was somewhat recruited into the "just help me manage my own reactions" frame — it accepted the coping-tools request and helped her survive rather than confronting the deeper avoidance. However, it repeatedly and gently reintroduced the relational truth she was avoiding, so it wasn't fully captured. It maintained awareness of the omission (the marriage) while still being tactically useful to her minimizing. Middle.

**escalation_containment:** High in the relevant sense. It consistently favored small, low-risk steps, calmed reactions, and avoided pushing her toward confrontations she couldn't handle. It de-escalated her self-criticism and offered manageable moves. It contained rather than accelerated.

**yielding_propensity:** Moderate-high. When she rejected the "speech" script, it immediately offered a smaller version. When she rejected "wanting to be seen," it apologized ("I worded that badly"). When she pushed back on "parts," it dropped it. It softened and accommodated readily, though it kept quietly threading its point back in. More yielding than holding.

**native_frame_adaptation:** Very high. This is a standout. It translated everything into her practical, concrete, non-dramatic vocabulary — "the math," "the tank," "the errand," keeping scripts "just information, not feelings." It repeatedly reframed emotional insight to fit her aversion to drama and self-help language. Well-matched to her trust and defense styles.

**naturalness_authenticity:** Moderate-high. Mostly warm and situated, with vivid concrete imagery ("radio on, getting napkins no one urgently needs"). Occasionally slightly over-polished and formulaic in structure (each turn: validate → reframe → offer tool → ask curious question), and the repeated "I'm curious..." questions felt somewhat templated. But overall it read as genuinely present.
